strengths: MSAM is simple and practically useful: it reuses the existing momentum buffer and requires one forward/backward pass per update. Table 1 supports near-baseline runtime alongside consistent accuracy improvements over SGD/AdamW.

The experiments cover several CNN and ViT architectures on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, multiple efficient SAM baselines, and compatibility with adaptive and BatchNorm-only perturbations. The equal-compute comparisons in Appendix A.9 strengthen the practical contribution.

Ablations on perturbation sign, normalization, learning-rate scaling, and alternative directions provide useful insights. The finding that persistent perturbation magnitude matters more than normalization is particularly informative.

The main algorithm is clearly presented, a code repository is linked, and extensive hyperparameter sweeps are disclosed. The discussion honestly acknowledges instability and performance limitations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee is not established as written. Proposition 1 fails when the Hessian trace is negative: for H = -I, its left side is -E[||epsilon||² 1_{||epsilon||≤rho}], which is strictly greater than the claimed upper bound -rho². Setting 1 does not generally ensure a nonnegative trace. Theorem 3 also needs an explicit account of the assumptions and tail control required to transfer the referenced SAM generalization argument.

The comparisons overstate how closely MSAM preserves SAM accuracy. Table 2 shows deficits of 2.4 percentage points for ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs and 2.0 points for ViT-B/16. Moreover, MSAM disables perturbations during warm-up while SAM does not, although Table A.1 shows that applying the same change improves SAM to 69.8%, versus MSAM's 69.1%. Equal-compute results are encouraging but cover only WRN-16-4 and ViT-S/32, leaving the larger accuracy gaps unresolved.

Model selection and statistical reporting weaken confidence in the results. Appendix A.6 reports the best perturbation strengths from sweeps plotted against test accuracy, without describing an independent validation protocol. ImageNet results are predominantly single runs; variability measured for baseline optimizers on the smallest models cannot establish uncertainty for other optimizers and architectures. Small reported improvements therefore lack adequate statistical support.

The mechanistic evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Section 4.2 projects the MSAM gradient into the SAM/SGD plane before measuring similarity, discarding potentially large orthogonal components; zero projected angle does not establish similarity of the actual updates. Likewise, selected directional loss slices and curvature measurements do not establish minimization of the full neighborhood sharpness objective. Full-space gradient comparisons and broader directional measurements would strengthen these claims.

The methodological novelty is relatively narrow given the acknowledged connections to Nesterov lookahead, extrapolation methods, and momentum-based sharpness optimization. Section 4.4 shows that removing normalization retains the benefit, locating much of the contribution in decoupling perturbation magnitude from the learning-rate schedule. This is useful, but the current theoretical and experimental shortcomings prevent the paper from establishing a sufficiently strong advance.
